To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
acetylcholine excites 81% of brain stem neurone in the rat and that this excitatory effect has a short latency.
acetylcholine can excite neurones in the brain stem, and that the short latency excitatory response is similar to the excitatory response to glutamate and the excitatory response of Renshawe cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of acetylcholine in the central nervous system.
the role of the ACh in brain stem neurones.
the effects of iontophoretically-applied drugs on single neurons in the brain stem.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ACh is a transmitter at the neuromuscular junction and in the central nervous system.
the short‐latency excitatory response to ACh is a fast excitatory response.
the short-latency excitatory response to iontophoretic acetylcholine is due to the release of endogenous acetylcholine and not to the action of acetylcholine itself.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ACh excites neurones in the brain stem by two mechanisms.
in the brain stem there are neurones which are excited by ACh and which are excited by glutamate.
ACh excites neurones of the rat brain stem, both directly by the short-latency type II mechanism, and indirectly by the longer-latency type I mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain stem is a very important part of the body that helps to regulate many functions.
the ACh receptor is a very complex and diverse molecule, and that there are a number of different types of ACh receptor that can be found in the body.
